title: Philip K. Dick's Metz speech claiming the Man in the High Castle world was real

tellings.quote: >> where you know he gave this famous speech uh in Mets France where he I think it was called um you know if you if you think this world sucks you should see the others or something

he had a famous speech in Metz, France, where he said, "We are living in a computer-programmed reality." And that's the the famous line. But then he said, "And the only clue we have to it is when some variable is changed. Some alteration occurs in our reality."
tellings.difference: Quotes the line 'We are living in a computer-programmed reality' and the point that a changed variable is the only clue, where the story's telling gives the speech's title as roughly 'if you think this world sucks you should see the others'.
tellings.link_reason: Both are about Philip K. Dick's 1977 speech in Metz, France.

as_told.title: Philip K. Dick's Metz speech: The Man in the High Castle as a real timeline

plain: In a speech in Metz, France, in 1977, the novelist Philip K. Dick is said to have claimed that the world of his novel The Man in the High Castle, a story in which Germany and Japan won World War II, was a real timeline and not just something he made up. Michels brings the speech up himself on two episodes. He recalls its title as something like "if you think this world sucks, you should see the others"; the speech is listed under the title "If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others", and the story dates it to 1977, while Michels says "1976 or" 1977. A researcher named Riz Virk tells it on another episode, without naming a source. He quotes the famous line, "We are living in a computer-programmed reality," and says Dick added that the only clue we have is "when some variable is changed." Virk goes further than Michels: in his telling, Dick believed the beings running the simulation reran history down another timeline because they liked this one better. If true, it would mean a famous writer believed history itself had been edited, and that his fiction was a memory of the version that was cut.
